extracted.intended_audience: general readers, writers, and students interested in the short story form
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for composing and understanding short stories: their length, form, characteristic elements (plot, character, mood), and publication/genre considerations. Useful for writers learning the form and students/scholars analysing short fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read-in-one-sitting / evoke a single effect or mood
rubrics_metrics.description: A classic definition is that one should be able to read it in one sitting; it focuses on a self-contained incident (or linked incidents) with the intent of evoking a single effect or mood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edgar Allan Poe's 'single effect' idea is cited; H. G. Wells describes the short story as making 'something very bright and moving' and notes a reading-aloud duration of 15–50 minutes. Use this criterion to judge brevity, unity of impression, and concentrated emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on a self-contained incident or linked incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: The short story 'focuses on a self-contained incident or series of linked incidents'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the narrative centers on a limited set of events rather than the extended arcs typical of novels; linked incidents should cohere toward the story's single effect or mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length / word-count categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Short stories have no set length, but word counts are typically anywhere from 1,000 to 4,000; some works classified as short stories have up to 15,000 words. Stories under 1,000 words are often 'flash fiction'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different genres/markets vary; for example, SFWA/Nebula defines short story as fewer than 7,500 words. Use length guidelines flexibly, and follow specific publication/submission guidelines when submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic structure and plot elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Short stories are often theorised through elements of dramatic structure: exposition, complication, rising action, crisis, climax and resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of brevity, short stories may or may not follow full classical structure; many begin in medias res. Evaluate presence and economy of these structural elements and whether they serve the story's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax, crisis and turning point
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots of short stories have a climax, crisis, or turning point — the decisive moment for the protagonist and commitment to action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how clearly and economically the story reaches and handles its decisive moment and whether that moment delivers emotional/intellectual payoff consonant with the story's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-driven versus plot-driven emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Some definitions (e.g., William Faulkner) see the short story as character-driven: the writer's job is to follow a character and record what they say and do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the depth and economy of characterization: even in brief form, characters should feel motivated and significant for the incident(s) depicted; weigh character revelation against plot action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal design versus 'slice of life' suggestiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate: some (Somerset Maugham) argue a short story 'must have a definite design' with point of departure, climax and point of test; others (Chekhov) argue it should be a suggestive 'slice of life' without rounded-off endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the story aims for a tightened, classical design or a suggestive, fragmentary approach; both are valid—judge coherence and intentionality rather than adherence to one model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity and open-endedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Short stories often feature ambiguity—whether in ending, characterisation, or meaning—and endings may be conclusive or open-ended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how ambiguity is used: does it enrich the single effect or frustrate resolution? Consider whether openness serves thematic or emotional aims rather than being accidental vagueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concision, concentration and intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: The short story is a concentrated, concise form of narrative and descriptive prose fiction, often producing an intense episodic or anecdotal effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the economy of language, scene selection, and the intensity of focus; look for spare, necessary details and avoidance of extraneous material that dilutes impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of literary techniques and narrative devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Short stories make use of plot, resonance and other dynamic components as in a novel, drawing from a pool of literary techniques (e.g., frame story, in medias res, foreshadowing, irony, symbolism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the effective deployment of devices (foreshadowing, Chekhov's gun, symbolism, point of view, unreliable narrator, etc.) and whether they contribute to the unity and effect rather than functioning as gimmicks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning 'in medias res' and handling of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern short stories only occasionally have an exposition; they more typically begin in the middle of the action (in medias res).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the story introduces necessary context economically—through implication, detail, and character action—rather than heavy exposition that slows the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market, genre and publication influences
rubrics_metrics.description: The shape of the short story reflects the demands of available markets for publication and the evolution of the publishing industry; submission guidelines and periodical formats affect length and form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating work, consider target market/genre norms (e.g., literary magazine, genre magazine) and submission guidelines; adapt length and conventions accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability and transmedial potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Short stories are sometimes adapted for radio, television or film, often rewritten by other writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the story's cinematic/sound/episodic elements and whether its structure and core incident lend themselves to adaptation, though adaptability is not a primary quality metric for literary worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic economy: hook; 'show, don't tell'
rubrics_metrics.description: Related stylistic guidance includes use of a hook, strong narrative voice, and 'show, don't tell'—techniques that create immediate engagement in a brief form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the effectiveness of opening lines/hooks, the balance of narration versus dramatization, and the sensory/active details that reveal character and situation rather than exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity of theme, resonance and moral/idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Short stories often aim to extrapolate an essence of experience or produce resonance—some definitions emphasise making 'some temporary sense of our common, turbulent journey'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether thematic material is concentrated and resonates beyond the immediate incident, without overexplaining; resonance should arise naturally from incident, character, and language.
